column3: Fever, pain and swelling in a breast-feeding mother is lactational infection progressing to abscess (S. aureus): ultrasound-guided aspiration plus flucloxacillin.
Fine linear branching microcalcification suggests DCIS; vacuum-assisted (stereotactic) biopsy samples calcifications more reliably than standard core biopsy.
A sudden painful discrete lump in a perimenopausal woman is a cyst; ultrasound confirms it and aspiration relieves it.
Bilateral cyclical pain and lumpiness worse before periods is ANDI (fibroadenosis/cyclical mastalgia): reassurance, a supportive bra and simple analgesia.
Several young relatives with breast cancer means genetic counselling and BRCA1/2 testing before planning surveillance or risk-reducing surgery.
A large, rapidly growing mass with stretched shiny skin in a woman over 40 is a phyllodes tumour; treat by wide excision with clear margins.
A hard enlarging lump with a spiculated mammographic mass is cancer until proven otherwise: core needle biopsy gives histology and receptor status.
A painless lump appearing after stopping breast-feeding is a galactocele (milk-retention cyst); aspiration of milky fluid is diagnostic and curative.
Breast enlargement in a pubertal boy is physiological gynaecomastia, which usually settles within 2 years; exclude drugs (e.g. cannabis) and hormonal causes.
Invasive lobular carcinoma is often multifocal and bilateral and underestimated on mammography, so MRI is used to define its extent before surgery.
Bilateral greenish-black multiduct discharge in a postmenopausal woman is duct ectasia; reassure if imaging is normal.
A painless, discrete, very mobile lump in a young woman is a fibroadenoma (‘breast mouse’); confirm with ultrasound and core biopsy.
A painless unilateral subareolar lump in a middle-aged man is male breast cancer until proven otherwise; gynaecomastia is usually bilateral, soft and tender.
A hard, irregular lump with axillary nodes in an elderly woman is breast carcinoma; confirm by triple assessment.
Nipple retraction with green-yellow discharge and dilated ducts on ultrasound is duct ectasia.
A smooth, highly mobile lump in a 21-year-old with benign cytology (C2) is a fibroadenoma.
A non-itchy eczema-like rash of the nipple and areola with an underlying mass is Paget disease of the nipple, usually with underlying carcinoma.
A tender, inflamed breast with fever 2 weeks postpartum and no mass is lactational mastitis; continue breast-feeding and give flucloxacillin.
A 92-year-old with ER-positive disease is treated with primary endocrine therapy (tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor) rather than surgery.
DCIS throughout all quadrants cannot be excised with conservation: mastectomy, with immediate reconstruction in a young woman.
A 2-cm ER-positive cancer with a clinically negative axilla: wide local excision and sentinel node biopsy, then radiotherapy and endocrine therapy.
I
Cytology-proven axillary nodes need axillary node clearance, and an ER-negative tumour in a young woman needs chemotherapy.
A
A firm lump with skin dimpling (tethering) in a 72-year-old is breast cancer; peau d’orange is skin oedema from lymphatic blockage, not a diagnosis.

A 34-year-old woman has lumpiness and tenderness in both breasts that is worse in the days before menstruation. An ultrasound scan shows multiple small cysts bilaterally, and a tissue sample shows fibrosis and epithelial hyperplasia.
A 28-year-old woman has a 1 cm soft, painless lump in her right breast that appeared suddenly last week; there is no other abnormality on examination.

A 42-year-old woman has a hard 2 cm lump in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast with axillary lymphadenopathy. She has had bilateral cosmetic breast augmentation, and the mammogram is too hazy to delineate any lesion.
A 52-year-old woman has a 4 cm lump in her left breast. Fine-needle aspiration cytology reports dysplastic cells.
A 45-year-old woman has a long-standing lump in her right breast. Ultrasound shows a cyst, which is aspirated under ultrasound guidance; the aspirate is blood-stained.

CA 15-3 is the breast cancer marker, used to monitor treatment and recurrence rather than for diagnosis.
Trastuzumab (anti-HER2) is given for HER2-positive breast cancer, especially node-positive disease, with chemotherapy.
Tamoxifen is a SERM: antagonist in the breast but agonist in the endometrium and clotting system (endometrial cancer, VTE).
Anastrozole, an aromatase inhibitor, blocks peripheral oestrogen synthesis and is used in postmenopausal ER-positive disease.
Trastuzumab causes (usually reversible) left ventricular dysfunction and can cause pulmonary toxicity, so LVEF is monitored.
Cyclophosphamide’s metabolite acrolein causes haemorrhagic cystitis and bladder cancer (mesna is protective).
A highly mobile lump in a young woman with benign cytology is a fibroadenoma.
I
An ill-defined, hot, red, tender area in a breast-feeding woman is lactational mastitis; a fluctuant mass would suggest abscess.
D
A hard, craggy lump after trauma with benign cytology is fat necrosis; it mimics carcinoma, so triple assessment is still needed.
C
Yellow-brown discharge from multiple ducts with a normal mammogram is duct ectasia.
B
A well-demarcated, fluctuant, transilluminable lump is a cyst; ultrasound and aspiration confirm it.
